name: Rabih az-Zubayr’s state
summary: A conquest state built by the Sudanese warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, who took Bornu (1893); French forces killed him at Kousséri in 1900.

location.value: Rabih moved his capital to Dikwa in Bornu, probably for better communications and water.

terrain.value: Flat Sahel and savanna plains around Lake Chad, with river floodplains along the Chari and Logone.

climate.value: Hot and dry, with a short rainy season in summer; desert to the north.

resources.value: Grain, cattle and horses, fish from Lake Chad, and captives taken in raids.

disasters.value: Famines and depopulation followed Rabih’s wars and heavy taxation in Bornu and Bagirmi.

population.value: The page gives no population figure.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal or market town.

migration.value: Rabih’s armies moved west from the Bahr el Ghazal in Sudan through Dar al-Kuti to Lake Chad.

economicBase.value: Rabih sought his fortune in the ivory and slave trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Saharan routes north to Tripoli and east to Wadai and Sudan, carrying slaves, ivory and guns.

wealth.value: Wealth came from plunder of Bornu and Bagirmi and the sale of captives for guns and supplies.

moneyAndTax.value: Tribute, cloth, cowries and trade goods.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above farmers; captives and slaves at the bottom.

governmentType.value: A military state: at its height Rabih's army was one of the best equipped in sub-Saharan Africa, with about 3,000 riflemen at Dikwa within perhaps 35,000 soldiers.

keyRulers.value: Born c. 1840 near Khartoum and enslaved as a child, Rabih served under the trader al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur; the beginning of his rule over Bornu is dated to 2 October 1893; his son Fadlallah was killed by the French at Gujba on 23 August 1901.

succession.value: Rabih’s son Fadlallah tried to carry on after 1900 but was killed by the French in 1901.

institutions.value: An army organised in companies of rifle-armed soldiers; Rabih kept some Bornu officials to collect taxes.

stability.value: Constant war; the state existed through conquest and lasted only about 20 years.

eliteConflict.value: Rabih’s hold over his commanders was strong; conquered Bornu nobles resented his rule.

armyAndTech.value: Perhaps 35,000 soldiers at its height, with a core of 3,000 fusiliers kept at Dikwa under Rabih’s own command.

majorWars.value: In 1892 Rabih beat a joint Bagirmi–Wadai army and drove Gaourang from Massenya; in 1893 he won at Amja (May) and Lekarawa and sacked Kukawa (about 3,000 killed and 4,000 captured); he died at the Battle of Kousséri on 22 April 1900, when Lamy was mortally wounded and Rabih’s forces were defeated.

territoryChange.value: Conquered Bagirmi and Bornu in 1893, sacking Kukawa and moving the capital to Dikwa.

alliancesRivals.value: Rabih fought Wadai, Bagirmi and Bornu, and finally France; he had ties to the Senussi of Dar al-Kuti.

inventions.value: No major inventions are recorded; the army relied on imported and captured rifles.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to trade for guns and supplies, but hostile to European advances.

communicationTransport.value: Caravan routes, horses, camels and porters linked the Lake Chad region with the Sahara and Sudan.

religion.value: Rabih accepted the authority of the Mahdist state in 1887 and saw himself as a disciple of the Mahdi; he restored Sharia-based justice in 1895. The page does not use the word Sunni.

languageWriting.value: Arabic for government and letters; Kanuri and many other local languages spoken by subjects.

artsArchitecture.value: Few remains; Rabih built a fortified palace at Dikwa, which partly survives.

socialStructure.value: Rabih and his commanders, slave soldiers, conquered officials, farmers and captives.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to Rabih and the army rather than to a shared people or tradition.

dailyLife.value: Village farming; cassava, millet or sorghum.

neighbours.value: Wadai, Bagirmi, Bornu, the Sokoto Caliphate, Dar al-Kuti, and French, British and German forces.

ideasReligions.value: Mahdist links: Rabih offered loyalty to the Mahdist state in Sudan, though he acted independently.

colonisation.value: French forces defeated and killed Rabih at the Battle of Kousséri in April 1900.

riseSignals.value: Rabih entered Bornu in the summer of 1893 after defeating a joint Bagirmi–Wadai army in 1892, and moved his capital to Dikwa.

peakPeriod.value: His army entered Bornu in the summer of 1893 (the conquest of Kanem–Bornu is dated 1892–94) and he moved his capital from Kukawa to Dikwa. He was killed at Kousséri on 22 April 1900.

declineSignals.value: French columns advanced on Lake Chad from 1899 and fought Rabih’s forces.

outcome.value: French forces under Lamy attacked his fortification at Lakhta on 22 April 1900 and Rabih was killed; the defeat opened the way to French colonisation of Chad.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
